uncited: Camera Matrix Ray Generation computes the origin and direction vectors for primary rays corresponding to each pixel in an image, based on explicit camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters.
It solves the problem of mapping 2D raster coordinates to 3D world-space rays for volume rendering or ray tracing.

It differs from [Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation](1319-orthographic-parallel-camera-ray-generation.md) by using perspective projection (converging rays) and from [Pinhole Camera Ray Generation](5058-pinhole-camera-ray-generation.md) by explicitly constructing and utilizing a calibration matrix $K$ rather than assuming a canonical pinhole model with unit focal length and center at the image center.
*   Image dimensions: Width $W$, Height $H$ (integers).
*   Camera Intrinsics: A 3x3 matrix $K$ (or parameters $f_x, f_y, c_x, c_y$).
*   Camera Extrinsic: A 4x4 Camera-to-World transformation matrix $T_{c2w}$ (or SE(3) pose).
*   Ray Origins: Tensor of shape $(H, W, 3)$ containing world-space origins.
*   Ray Directions: Tensor of shape $(H, W, 3)$ containing world-space directions (often normalized).
The upper-left 3x3 block is the rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}_{c2w}$.
The rightmost column (indices 0-2 of column 3) is the translation vector $\mathbf{t}_{c2w}$ (camera origin in world space).
Create 2D grids of pixel coordinates $(i, j)$ for $i \in [0, W)$ and $j \in [0, H)$.
*   Pixel Centering: Add 0.5 to coordinates to target the center of each pixel: $i' = i + 0.5, j' = j + 0.5$.
Calculate the unnormalized direction vector in the camera's local coordinate system.
The camera typically looks down the negative Z-axis (OpenGL convention) or positive Z-axis (OpenCV convention).
Rotate the camera-space directions into world space using the rotation part of the camera-to-world matrix.
Normalize $\mathbf{d}_{\text{world}}$ to unit length.
The ray origin is the camera position in world space, extracted from the translation component of $T_{c2w}$.
Constructs the 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix $K$ assuming zero skew and aspect ratio of 1.
This simplification assumes square pixels and a principal point at the image center.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(W \times H)$ to generate rays for all pixels.
The operations are element-wise vector math, highly parallelizable on GPU.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(W \times H)$ to store the origin and direction tensors.
*   **Strengths:** Explicit control over camera calibration; supports arbitrary principal points and focal lengths; standard in NeRF and modern rendering pipelines.
*   **Limitations:** Requires accurate calibration data; sensitive to errors in $K$ or $T_{c2w}$; division by zero if focal length is 0.
*   **When to use:** When camera parameters are known from calibration (e.g., COLMAP, sensor data) or when precise control over projection geometry is needed.
*   **When not to use:** For simple orthographic views or when only relative camera motion is available without scale/intrinsics.
Originating from standard computer graphics and photogrammetry, this method formalizes the pinhole camera model using matrix algebra.
The explicit use of the intrinsic matrix $K$ allows for handling non-square pixels and off-center principal points, generalizing the basic pinhole model.
